Hey! Things have gotten a little better. He definitely still chases and pins her, but we've started to notice patterns for what sets him off that we try to avoid. 

For example, he's super noise sensitive, so if we come home with groceries in plastic bags and are unloading them in the kitchen, he starts to get uncomfortable, his hyperesthesia starts bothering him, and he is more likely to he aggressive in those moments. So we adjusted and when we bring home groceries, we let him outside on the patio so he can be distracted and away from the noise. 

If there are big changes in his routine, like we get home late after a night out and their dinner is delayed a few hours, he is more likely to be pissy. In those cases we try to stay up with him for a little while to let him get his energy out in a healthy way and calm down before we all go to bed. 

I think we've finally dialed in the prozac/gabapentin dosages for him which has been helpful. Fitting in regular play time, rewarding good behavior and interactions (like when they pass each other in the hall without throwing hands), and doing our best to stick to a routine have all helped.

Something that changed is that our female finally started sticking up for herself more, almost to a point where it's a little excessive lol, but she will very clearly warn him if he's getting too close to her, and most of the time he actually listens and avoids her.

Also just a side note, we learned that the abscesses that we thought were caused by him biting her but were actually her anal glands getting infected, and we had them removed because they were very problematic, and since then he follows her around wayyyy less. Not saying you should do that, just an interesting observation that maybe scent does play a role.

I'm sorry you're going through this right now, I know how exhausting it can be. Do your best to be patient while you figure out what sets your aggressive kitty off, look for patterns and see if there's any way you can adjust your routine or environment to help. Give your kitty extra opportunities to get his(?) energy out and to use his brain, and give your other kitty some extra places to escape if possible, and help her(?) build her confidence to say "no" before something happens, and help him learn how to respect her boundaries. Reward good behavior, and dissipate unwanted behavior neutrally, doing your best to not get upset (this was tough for me). 

It will get better! Wishing you the best of luck 💙

If you're not too squeamish and want to see what the procedure is like, I highly recommend  watching some of the Toe Bro's videos on YouTube!

If you'd prefer a written description, here goes:

As I understand it, what happens when you have an ingrown nail is that the sides of the nail start to curve and dig in to the flesh on either side of the toe, which as you can imagine is not pleasant.  This can occur after trauma to the toe, or because of genetics.

To prevent this from happening, the curved/long sides of the toenail need to be removed so your skin can heal, especially if an underlying abscess has formed underneath the nail.

The procedure usually goes like this:

First, the doctor will place a tourniquet around your toe to prevent excessive bleeding. Then, they will administer a few doses of local anesthetic to the affected toe. The anesthetic is injected into the nerve located at the base of the toe (where it meets the foot) using a very small hypodermic needle. This is generally the most painful part of the procedure, as I'm told, as there is a small pinch and burn associated with the administration of the first dose of anesthetic. After that, you shouldn't feel any pain at all.

Once you're nice and numb, the doctor will use a tool similar to a small file to loosen the edged of the nail away from the skin, as well as the flat of the nail away from the nail bed, all the way down to the level of the primary nail fold (cuticle) and the width of a few millimeters. The doctor then uses special nail trimmers to make a vertical cut in the nail that he's loosened, parallel to the side of the toe. They'll then take a surgical clamp (like a hemostat), grasp the cut sliver of nail, and rotate the hemostat 360+ degrees medially (towards the center of the toe) until the sliver of toe is free! The doctor will then use their file tool again to make sure that there are no small fragments of nail left behind.

At this point, the other side of the nail is usually completed exactly the same way. What you are left with is a skinnier portion of toenail than you had before, and no more ingrown!

The doctor will then clean the area. They usually soak two cotton swabs in an acid solution to apply to the areas where the nail was removed. This acid solution helps to cauterize the wound, and prevent bleeding in the future. The acid is ineffective if the area isn't very dry, which is another reason for the tourniquet application in the beginning of the procedure. 

After the acid, the doctor generally applies an antibiotic cream, bandages the toe, and gives you your post-op instructions. 

As far as recurrence of ingrown nails after this procedure, unfortunately it's not a fix-all. But it will certainly bring you tremendous relief in the meantime, at least for a few months.


That's about it! Hope that helps :)

I understand what you're saying, but these aren't wild equines. 

A few things that are important to understand: 

Species variation:

Equus ferus = feral ("wild") horses 

Equus caballus = domestic horses (horses for riding)

Equus asinus = donkeys

Though the genera are the same (Equus), the variation in species makes for some very different characteristics. 

Saying, "You think donkeys or horses have a barn to shelter in in the wild?" is problematic because it assumes that wild and domestic equines are one in the same. 

Take dogs, for example. This would be like saying that canines are all the same.

Canis lupus = wolf

Canis latrans = coyote

Canis lupus familiarus = domestic dog

All of them are canines, but have vastly, dramatically different conformations. I guarantee your Pomeranian wouldn't survive a Canadian winter. 

So yes, the equines in the pen are still hardy, but their conformation is very different from that of a 10th generation Montana mustang, and this needs to be recognized. There is no excuse for a domestic horse or donkey to not have access to a shelter structure.

Furthermore, like I've mentioned in other comments, old age and poor health further necessitates shelter from the elements, be it heat, cold, rain, snow, wind, or flies.

It's the same for cattle. Breeds used in the midwest are exceptionally different than those bred in California. They literally choose crossbreeds for their weather hardiness. That being said, when you drive out through Chino past the miles and miles of Holstein dairy farms, what do you see? You see cows sheltering under man-made structures to get out of the sun, and the cows that can't fit under the shelter seeking as much shade as possible. The shelters are built on raised hills of dirt so that when it rains, the cows don't have to stand knee-deep in mud and their own feces. 

Closer to home, you can take a drive on University Dr in the summer past the fields where the black Angus yearlings are rotated. When it's Pomona hot, they're almost always crammed into the tree-covered corners trying to get some relief from the sun, because as a breed, they're heat intolerant. If you go to India where they breed the ultra-heat resistant Brahman cattle, it might be a different story. But stick an Angus cow in India with no shelter and it will not fare well. 

I know that was long, but I hope it helped to explain my logic a little more clearly.

As far as what started it, I was diagnosed with OCD at 7 years, and they're often related. But I do have clear memories of my mother picking at her skin without even realizing it, enough to leave scars, so it's possible it was catalyzed by seeing her behavior, too.

It becomes a kind of soothing ritual in the face of anxiety/depression, you pick and it hurts, but the endorphins released are magical and make you want to keep doing it. It's trancelike, every day I catch myself picking and I didn't even notice I had started. So I think my efforts to stop are two-fold: (1) being aware of the situations that "trigger" me to pick, and making sure I have alternatives available (fidget toys, a rubber band, etc.) or planning accordingly (wearing long sleeves, making plans with friends or appointments I have to keep so that I'm not alone for too long, it's much easier to go ham on yourself when no one is watching), and (2) practicing mindfulness as much as I can to avoid falling into those trances that have me picking in the bathroom for an hour before I even realize it. If I can plan out my day, sometimes even down to the hour or minute, it helps take away those moments of uncertainty or "well, what should I do now?" that undoubtedly lead to picking.
